title: TLS 1.3 — Implement the Handshake from Scratch

questions.question: In HKDF (RFC 5869), what is the output of HKDF-Extract(salt, IKM) called and what does it represent?
options: PRK; a pseudorandom key derived via HMAC keyed by the salt
OKM; the final variable-length output bytes produced by HKDF-Expand
Transcript hash; the hash of all handshake messages so far
Traffic key; the AEAD encryption key used to protect records
questions.explanation: HKDF-Extract outputs a PRK (pseudorandom key), computed as HMAC(salt, IKM), which is then used by HKDF-Expand.

questions.question: What is the transcript hash used for in the TLS 1.3 key schedule?
options: To bind derived secrets to the exact handshake messages exchanged so far
To compress the TLS record header so records are smaller on the wire
To replace certificate signatures (Finished makes signatures unnecessary)
To generate the server's long-term private key deterministically
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 uses Transcript-Hash(messages) as context in Derive-Secret so derived secrets depend on the exact handshake transcript.

questions.question: TLS 1.3 HKDF-Expand-Label encodes an HkdfLabel as: uint16(L) || uint8(label_len) || label || uint8(context_len) || context. In the RFC 8448 example info bytes for deriving a 16-byte key begin with: 00 10 09 74 6c 73 31 33 20 6b 65 79 00. What does the 0x09 represent?
options: The length of the ASCII string "tls13 key" in bytes
The length of the derived key (16) modulo 256
The TLS version number encoded as a single byte
The number of handshake messages hashed so far
questions.explanation: 00 10 is the output length (16). 09 is the label length in bytes, and the label bytes are the ASCII string "tls13 key".

questions.question: How is the Finished key computed in TLS 1.3 for a given handshake traffic secret?
options: finished_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(traffic_secret, "finished", "", HashLen)
finished_key = HKDF-Extract(traffic_secret, Transcript-Hash(messages))
finished_key = SHA-256(traffic_secret || Transcript-Hash(messages))
finished_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(traffic_secret, "key", Transcript-Hash(messages), key_length)
questions.explanation: The Finished key is derived from the sender's handshake traffic secret using the fixed label "finished" and an empty context.

questions.question: For the client's Finished verify_data, which handshake messages are included in the Transcript-Hash input?
options: All handshake messages up to (but not including) the client's Finished, including the server's Finished
Only ClientHello and ServerHello (everything else is encrypted, so it can't be hashed)
Only the messages sent by the client (client-only transcript)
All handshake messages including the client's Finished (so it authenticates itself)
questions.explanation: Finished authenticates the transcript up to that point; the client's Finished includes the server's Finished in the transcript hash, but not itself.

questions.question: When deriving the handshake traffic key and IV from a traffic secret in TLS 1.3, what context is passed to HKDF-Expand-Label for the labels "key" and "iv"?
options: An empty byte string (zero-length context)
The transcript hash up to ServerHello
The full transcript bytes (concatenated messages)
The record sequence number encoded as bytes
questions.explanation: Traffic key calculation uses HKDF-Expand-Label with labels "key" and "iv" and a zero-length context; the transcript binding happens at the traffic-secret level.

questions.question: An active attacker flips one bit in the server's Certificate message in flight. Assuming signatures and hashes are secure, what should happen in TLS 1.3?
options: The client detects the change because Finished verify_data won't verify (transcript hash changes)
The client decrypts the rest of the handshake but silently ignores the certificate corruption
The handshake still succeeds because traffic secrets are derived only from DH
Only application data is affected; the handshake is not authenticated
questions.explanation: Finished is a MAC over the transcript hash under a key derived from the handshake traffic secret, so transcript modifications are detected.

questions.question: In HKDF-Extract, what does "salt not provided" mean in RFC 5869 / TLS-style usage?
options: Use HashLen bytes of zeros as the salt
Use the IKM as the salt and also as the message
Skip Extract and run Expand directly on the IKM
Use a random salt generated per call
questions.explanation: RFC 5869 defines that if salt is not provided, it is treated as a string of HashLen zeros.
